description: v are building a medical host for space mission
summary:
REET is an AI-assisted medical platform that helps astronaut crews stay healthy when Earth can’t respond in real time. On Mars, a message takes 4 to 24 minutes each way, and the link can drop completely.

What we built: a software prototype. It learns each astronaut’s personal baseline and flags persistent changes with a clear explanation. A rule-based emergency engine runs separately from the AI and shows step-by-step procedures offline. A delay-tolerant Earth link queues consultations through blackouts. An onboard assistant answers from sourced knowledge, refuses dosing questions and escalates uncertain cases. All data in the prototype is simulated and labelled.

Future development: a REET wristband and camera system. This would include contactless breathing and heart rate from a camera, skin and core temperature sensing, and blood-cell and biomarker checks. It would also include location mapping, so astronauts can navigate a habitat or spacewalk and not get lost.
details:
What it does and how it works

REET is an AI-assisted medical system for astronaut crews. It is designed for missions where doctors on Earth can’t answer in real time, such as Mars, where a message takes 4 to 24 minutes each way.

The software prototype works in five steps:

  1. Collects data. It takes heart rate, breathing, oxygen, temperature and cabin air readings from a simulator, a webcam, or a Bluetooth watch. Every value is labelled measured, simulated, AI-generated or doctor-confirmed.
  2. Learns each person’s normal. It builds a personal baseline for every astronaut and flags persistent changes with a plain-language explanation and a confidence score.
  3. Runs an emergency engine. Fixed rules, separate from the AI, detect dangers such as low oxygen or unsafe air. They show step-by-step procedures even with no Earth link.
  4. Handles delayed communication. Consultations are queued with the latest vitals, survive blackouts, and return the doctor’s reply later. Moon and Mars delays can be simulated at high speed.
  5. Answers questions safely. An onboard assistant replies from a sourced knowledge base, shows its confidence, refuses medicine-dose questions and escalates what it can’t answer.

Benefits

  • Gives a crew medical support that doesn’t depend on Earth.
  • Catches slow health changes that fixed “normal ranges” would miss.
  • Keeps working through delays, blackouts and AI failure.
  • Makes every alert explainable, so crews can judge how far to trust it.

Intended impact

REET aims to lower medical risk on long missions, where radiation, muscle and bone loss, poor sleep and cabin CO₂ build up and evacuation isn’t possible. The same design could support remote clinics, polar bases, ships and disaster zones.

Tools and technology

  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Vercel hosting
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLite (PostgreSQL later), WebSockets, JWT login
  • Browser features: webcam estimation of heart and breathing rate (computed locally), Web Bluetooth for watch heart rate, phone motion sensors
  • Development: AI coding assistants, used to build and test the prototype
  • Hardware: none yet. The prototype is software only.

Future hardware (not built yet)

A REET wristband and camera system with contactless breathing and heart rate, skin temperature from a thermal sensor, and blood and biomarker checks from a separate analyser. It would also add location mapping so astronauts can navigate a habitat or spacewalk without getting lost. Core body temperature and blood counts can’t be measured by a wristband today, so these need dedicated hardware and clinical validation.

What makes it creative

  • It treats the wearable as replaceable and puts the value in the system around it.
  • It is built for delay and blackout, not for a constant connection.
  • The emergency engine is deliberately independent of the AI.
  • Provenance labels stop simulated data being mistaken for real data.
